title: Why Code Review & What to Look For
summary: Code review exists to catch what tests and CI can't: design drift, missing context, and single-owner knowledge. Learn what a reviewer should actually evaluate and what they aren't on the hook for.

slides.markdown:
Every merged pull request went through at least one pair of eyes that wasn't the author's. That gate is **code review**, and it is one of the few practices almost every engineering org agrees on — yet most engineers can't say precisely what it's *for*.

It is not a spell-check pass for style, and it is not a re-derivation of the whole design from scratch. It is the mechanism a team uses to catch correctness bugs a compiler can't see, keep the codebase's design coherent across dozens of contributors, and spread knowledge so no single person is a single point of failure.

Get the purpose wrong and you get the two failure modes that plague most teams: rubber-stamp approvals that catch nothing, or gatekeeping that blocks everything. This topic sets the actual bar.

Code review earns its cost by doing four things at once, and a good reviewer keeps all four in mind rather than fixating on one:

- **Correctness** — catching a bug the author's own testing missed, especially edge cases the author was too close to see.
- **Design fit** — does this change belong here, does it duplicate something that exists, does it paint the codebase into a corner.
- **Knowledge-sharing** — a second person now understands this code, so the author isn't the only one who can safely change it later.
- **Shared ownership** — an approval is the team saying "we accept this as ours," not just the author's. That changes how bugs get triaged later: nobody gets to say "not my code."

Miss the last two and review looks like pure overhead. They're the reason teams keep doing it even when tests already catch most bugs.

slides.subTitle: What to actually evaluate, in order
slides.markdown:
A reviewer scanning a diff without a mental checklist tends to fixate on whatever catches the eye first — usually naming. Work through these in roughly this order instead:

1. **Correctness** — does the logic do what the description claims, including edge cases (empty input, concurrent access, the error path)?
2. **Tests** — do they cover the change, and would they actually fail if the logic broke? A test that can't fail is worse than no test.
3. **Design fit** — does this belong in this module, does it duplicate existing logic, does it lock in an interface that's expensive to change later?
4. **Security** — new external input, an auth check that moved, a secret that shouldn't be logged.
5. **Performance** — an obviously quadratic loop over user data, a query added inside a loop.
6. **Readability** — last, not first: a correct, well-tested, well-designed change with an awkward variable name is a one-line nit, not a blocker.

Ordering matters: leading with readability is how real bugs slip through underneath a wall of style comments.

Reviewers routinely spend most of their time on the category that matters least. Split the two explicitly:

| | Reviewing for bugs | Reviewing for style |
|---|---|---|
| **What it catches** | logic errors, missed edge cases, race conditions | naming, formatting, brace placement |
| **Who should do it** | a human, every time | a linter/formatter, every time |
| **Cost if skipped** | production incident | mildly inconsistent diff |
| **Consistency** | judgement-based, varies by reviewer | 100% consistent once configured |

If your team argues about tabs vs spaces or import ordering in PR comments, that's a tooling gap, not a review discipline gap — `prettier`, `black`, `gofmt`, and a CI lint step settle it before a human ever opens the diff. That frees reviewer attention for the column on the left, which no tool can check.

A diff view shows red and green lines, but a change only makes sense against the file it landed in. Reviewing red/green lines in isolation is how reviewers approve code that's individually fine and collectively wrong.

Before commenting, pull up:

- **The whole modified function**, not just the changed lines — a renamed variable can be correct on the diff line and wrong three lines below it, outside the diff context window.
- **The call sites**, if the change touches a shared function's signature or behavior — does every caller still hold?
- **Recent history on the file**, if something looks odd — `git blame` often reveals the line was written that way to work around a bug, and removing it silently reintroduces it.

This is slower than skimming the diff top to bottom, which is exactly why it's the step people skip under time pressure — and exactly the step that catches the bugs a fast skim can't.

slides.sectionTitle: What reviewers are not on the hook for
slides.markdown:
Review has a scope, and exceeding it is as harmful as falling short of it. A reviewer is **not** responsible for:

- **Re-deriving the whole design from scratch.** If the approach was agreed in a design doc or a prior discussion, review isn't the place to relitigate it — that's what the design-review gate is for, and doing it here as a surprise wastes the author's work and the reviewer's time.
- **Guaranteeing zero bugs.** Review raises the odds of catching a bug; it doesn't certify their absence. Tests, monitoring, and production observability carry the rest of that job.
- **Personally being able to write a better version.** "I'd have done it differently" is not a blocking comment unless the difference matters to correctness or maintainability — taste alone isn't a veto.

A reviewer who treats every PR as a chance to redesign the system burns trust fast, and teams respond by routing around them.

The healthiest mental model: review is a **second author's confidence check**, not an obstacle course the first author has to survive.

A gate mindset produces adversarial PRs — the author writes defensively, the reviewer looks for reasons to say no, and every comment reads as a challenge. A confidence mindset produces the opposite: the reviewer's job is to get to a genuine "yes, I'd stand behind this shipping," and most comments are questions rather than demands.

This shows up concretely in comment phrasing. "This needs a null check" reads as a gate. "What happens if this list is empty — did you consider that?" reads as a second engineer thinking it through with you. Same concern, opposite relationship to the author. The next topic in this group goes deep on exactly this framing.

slides.subTitle: Approving without reading
slides.markdown:
A rubber-stamp approval is a green checkmark left by someone who skimmed the diff title, maybe glanced at the file list, and clicked approve. It happens for predictable reasons: review queues are backed up, the author is trusted, the diff looks large and unglamorous, or the reviewer assumes CI already caught anything real.

The cost compounds silently. Each rubber-stamped PR trains the author that review adds no friction and no value, so quality quietly drifts — and the team's *belief* that changes are reviewed becomes false at exactly the moment an incident makes that gap visible.

A concrete tell: if a reviewer can't name one thing they checked beyond "it compiled and CI is green," it wasn't a review. The fix isn't more process, it's smaller PRs and honest capacity limits — see the *Review Process & Tooling* topic in this group for both.

A small diff, and what a checklist-driven review catches that a skim misses.

```diff
 def apply_discount(price, code):
-    return price * DISCOUNTS[code]
+    discount = DISCOUNTS.get(code, 1.0)
+    return price * discount
```

Skim reaction: "nice, handles unknown codes now, LGTM."

Checklist reaction:
- **Correctness** — an unknown code now silently charges full price instead of raising. Is that the intended behavior, or should an invalid code be rejected upstream with an error?
- **Tests** — is there a test for an unknown code specifically, or only for the happy path?
- **Design fit** — should this fallback live here, or should `DISCOUNTS` be validated once at the API boundary so every caller benefits?

Same two lines, three real questions. None of them are about naming or formatting — they're exactly the correctness and design-fit checks from the ordered list earlier in this topic.

Not every diff deserves the full checklist at full depth. A senior reviewer calibrates effort to blast radius:

- **Payment, auth, and data-migration code** — read every line, trace call sites, ask about rollback.
- **A new internal admin-only script** — correctness and an obvious footgun check, not a design deep-dive.
- **A one-line config bump** — confirm the value and where it's used; that's most of the risk.

Spending twenty minutes on a config typo fix and two minutes on a schema migration is the calibration inverted, and it's a common trap for newer reviewers who default to "same depth every time" because it feels fair. It isn't fair to the team — it's a fixed budget spent on the wrong line items. Risk-based depth is what lets a reviewer keep up with volume without becoming a rubber stamp.

This topic covered *what* review is for and *what* to check. The rest of the group builds out the practice around it: writing feedback that improves code without damaging the relationship, receiving feedback (including disagreement) professionally, structuring the process itself so review scales with team size, the recognizable anti-patterns that erode trust in review, and the real-time alternatives — pairing and async collaboration across timezones — that complement or replace it.

The throughline across all of it: review works when it's a second engineer's genuine confidence check on the code, calibrated to risk, and it fails the same two ways regardless of tooling — nobody actually looking, or looking at the wrong things.
